chapters.title: Kinematics
chapters.notes: Acceleration describes the rate of change of velocity. For constant acceleration, use v = u + at. Starting from rest means u = 0; displacement and velocity are different quantities.

chapters.title: Laws of Motion
chapters.notes: Net external force equals mass times acceleration. Resolve forces before applying F = ma. Mass measures inertia; acceleration depends on the net force, not the largest individual force.

chapters.title: Work, Energy & Power
chapters.notes: Translational kinetic energy is one half of mass times speed squared. Doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy. The work done by the net force equals the change in kinetic energy.

chapters.title: Gravitation
chapters.notes: Outside a spherical Earth, gravitational acceleration varies inversely with the square of distance from the centre. At height h, that distance is R+h, not h. At h = R, gravity is one quarter of its surface value.

chapters.title: Electrostatics
chapters.notes: The magnitude of the electrostatic force is k times the product of charge magnitudes divided by separation squared. Convert microcoulombs to coulombs. Increasing separation weakens the force according to an inverse-square law.

chapters.title: Current Electricity
chapters.notes: For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, current equals potential difference divided by resistance. Current is measured in amperes, voltage in volts and resistance in ohms. Increasing resistance at fixed voltage lowers current.

chapters.title: Ray Optics
chapters.notes: A thin converging lens forming a real image obeys 1/f = 1/u + 1/v when u and v are positive distance magnitudes. Therefore f = uv/(u+v). With Cartesian signs, the equivalent formula is 1/f = 1/v - 1/u.

chapters.title: Thermodynamics
chapters.notes: With heat added to the gas positive and work done by the gas positive, the first law is delta U = Q - W. Heat supplied may partly increase internal energy and partly be transferred as work. State the sign convention first.
